name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q01 - Elemental composition of living and inanimate matter

questiontext.text: It is said that elemental composition of living organisms and that of inanimate objects (like earth's crust) are similar in the sense that all the major elements are present in both. Then what would be the difference between these two groups? Choose a correct answer from among the following:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Elemental analysis of living tissues and non-living matter such as the earth's crust shows that both contain the same major elements, including carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur, calcium, and magnesium.

Step 2: Evaluation
Although the qualitative list of elements is similar, their relative abundance per unit mass differs markedly. Living organisms have a much higher relative abundance of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen compared to any inanimate object such as the earth's crust, because organic biomolecules (carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids) and water form the bulk of living matter.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the key difference is that living organisms have more carbon, oxygen and hydrogen per unit mass than inanimate objects.

answer.text: Living organisms have more gold in them than inanimate objects.
Living organisms have more water in their body than inanimate objects.
Living organisms have more carbon, oxygen and hydrogen per unit mass than inanimate objects.
Living organisms have more calcium in them than inanimate objects.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q02 - Element not found in living organisms

questiontext.text: Many elements are found in living organisms either free or in the form of compounds. Which of the following is not found in living organisms?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Living tissues contain several inorganic elements either in free ionic form or as parts of organic and inorganic compounds. Essential elements in human and animal tissues include sodium, magnesium, calcium, and iron.

Step 2: Evaluation
Magnesium is a key cofactor for enzymes and is present in chlorophyll; iron is essential for haemoglobin and cytochromes; sodium is a major extracellular cation involved in nerve impulse transmission and osmotic balance. In contrast, silicon is abundant in the earth's crust (as silicates) but is present in negligible amounts and is not found as a major constituent of living organisms.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, silicon is the element not found in living organisms among the given choices.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q03 - Identification of an amino acid

questiontext.text: Aminoacids, have both an amino group and a carboxyl group in their structure. Which one of the following is an amino acid?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Amino acids are substituted methanes containing an amino group (\(-\text{NH}_2\)), a carboxyl group (\(-\text{COOH}\)), a hydrogen atom, and a variable R-group attached to the same \(\alpha\)-carbon.

Step 2: Evaluation
Formic acid (\(\text{HCOOH}\)) and glycolic acid (\(\text{HOCH}_2\text{COOH}\)) are carboxylic acids lacking an amino group. Glycerol is a trihydroxy alcohol (trihydroxypropane) with no amino or carboxyl group. Glycine (\(\text{H}_2\text{N}-\text{CH}_2-\text{COOH}\)) is the simplest amino acid, where the variable R-group is a hydrogen atom.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, glycine is an amino acid.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q04 - Zwitterionic form of an amino acid

questiontext.text: An aminoacid under certain conditions have both positive and negative charges simultaneously in the same molecule. Such a form of aminoacid is called

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Amino acids possess ionisable functional groups: a basic amino group (\(-\text{NH}_2\)) and an acidic carboxyl group (\(-\text{COOH}\)). Their ionisation state depends on the pH of the surrounding solution.

Step 2: Evaluation
In solutions of different pH, the structure of an amino acid changes. At a specific pH (isoelectric point), the carboxyl group loses a proton to become negatively charged (\(-\text{COO}^-\)) while the amino group accepts a proton to become positively charged (\(-\text{NH}_3^+\)). This dipolar ion carrying both positive and negative charges simultaneously, with a net charge of zero, is known as a zwitterionic form.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, such a form of an amino acid is called the zwitterionic form.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q05 - Identification of a hexose sugar

questiontext.text: Sugars are technically called carbohydrates, referring to the fact that their formulae are only multiple of C(H2O). Hexoses therefore have six carbons, twelve hydrogens and six oxygen atoms. Glucose is a hexose. Choose from among the following another hexose.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Monosaccharides are classified according to the number of carbon atoms they contain. A hexose is a six-carbon monosaccharide with the general molecular formula \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6\).

Step 2: Evaluation
Erythrose is a four-carbon sugar (tetrose). Ribose and ribulose are five-carbon sugars (pentoses). Fructose, like glucose, is a six-carbon sugar (ketohexose) with the molecular formula \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, fructose is another hexose.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q06 - Formation of nucleotide from nucleoside

questiontext.text: When you take cells or tissue pieces and grind them with an acid in a mortar and pestle, all the small biomolecules dissolve in the acid. Proteins, polysaccharides and nucleic acids are insoluble in mineral acid and get precipitated. The acid soluble compounds include aminoacids, nucleosides, small sugars etc. When one adds a phosphate group to a nucleoside, one gets another acid soluble biomolecule called

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Nucleic acids are built from monomeric units that consist of three components: a heterocyclic nitrogenous base, a monosaccharide (pentose sugar), and a phosphate group.

Step 2: Evaluation
When a nitrogenous base is linked to a pentose sugar, the resulting compound is called a nucleoside (for example, adenosine or guanosine). When a phosphate group is esterified to the sugar of a nucleoside, the resulting phosphorylated compound is called a nucleotide (for example, adenylic acid or guanylic acid), which is also found in the acid-soluble pool.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, adding a phosphate group to a nucleoside yields a nucleotide.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q07 - Cellular fraction represented by acid soluble pool

questiontext.text: When we homogenise any tissue in an acid the acid soluble pool represents

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Chemical analysis of living tissue using trichloroacetic acid separates cellular components into two fractions: the acid-soluble pool (filtrate) and the acid-insoluble pool (retentate).

Step 2: Evaluation
The acid-soluble pool contains small molecules with molecular weights ranging from about 18 to 800 daltons, which roughly represents the cytoplasmic composition (cytosol containing amino acids, monosaccharides, nucleotides, and inorganic ions). In contrast, macromolecules from the cytoplasm and organelles (such as cell membranes, nucleus, and mitochondria) form the acid-insoluble fraction.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the acid-soluble pool represents the cytoplasm.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q08 - Most abundant component of living organisms

questiontext.text: The most abundant component of living organisms is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Living cells consist of both inorganic and organic chemical components in specific proportions by total cellular mass.

Step 2: Evaluation
According to average cellular composition, water constitutes approximately 70–90% of the total cellular mass, making it the single most abundant chemical in living organisms. Proteins account for 10–15%, nucleic acids for 5–7%, and carbohydrates (sugars) for about 3%.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, water is the most abundant component of living organisms.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q09 - Number of monomer types in proteins

questiontext.text: A homopolymer has only one type of building block called monomer repeated 'n' number of times. A heteropolymer has more than one type of monomer. Proteins are heteropolymers usually made of

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Proteins are polypeptides, which are linear chains of amino acids linked together by peptide bonds.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because proteins are formed from multiple different amino acids rather than a single repeating amino acid, they are heteropolymers. In living organisms, there are 20 standard types of amino acids (such as alanine, cysteine, proline, tryptophan, lysine, etc.) that serve as the monomeric building blocks of proteins.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, proteins are heteropolymers usually made of 20 types of monomers.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q10 - Physiological functions discharged by proteins

questiontext.text: Proteins perform many physiological functions. For example, some functions as enzymes. Which of the following represents an additional function that some proteins discharge?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Proteins carry out diverse biological roles in living organisms, acting as enzymes, structural components, transport molecules, receptors, antibodies, and hormones.

Step 2: Evaluation
Some hormones (such as insulin and growth hormone) are proteinaceous in nature and regulate physiological processes. In contrast, antibiotics, melanin (skin pigment), and anthocyanins or carotenoids (flower pigments) are secondary metabolites or non-proteinaceous compounds rather than proteins.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, functioning as hormones represents an additional physiological function discharged by some proteins.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q11 - Monomer unit of glycogen homopolymer

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Polysaccharides are long chains of monosaccharide units linked by glycosidic bonds. Homopolymers consist of only one type of monosaccharide unit.

Step 2: Evaluation
Glycogen is the major storage polysaccharide in animals and is a branched homopolymer composed exclusively of \(\alpha\)-D-glucose units linked by \(\alpha\)-1,4-glycosidic bonds in the linear chains and \(\alpha\)-1,6-glycosidic bonds at the branch points. Galactose, ribose, and amino acids are not the monomers of glycogen.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, glycogen is a homopolymer made of glucose units.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q12 - Number of ends in a glycogen molecule

questiontext.text: The number of 'ends' in a glycogen molecule would be

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Glycogen is a highly branched polysaccharide of glucose. An unbranched linear polysaccharide chain has two ends: one reducing end (right end) and one non-reducing end (left end).

Step 2: Evaluation
When a branch is added to the main chain via an \(\alpha\)-1,6-glycosidic linkage, the new branch terminates in an additional non-reducing end, while the single reducing end remains unchanged. Thus, each branch contributes one extra non-reducing end. If there are \(b\) branches, there are \(b\) non-reducing ends from the branches, one non-reducing end from the main chain, and one reducing end—wait: in a tree-like polymer with \(n\) chains (main chain + \(b\) branches), the main chain starts at the single reducing end and ends at one non-reducing end, and each branch adds one more non-reducing end, giving \(b + 1\) non-reducing ends and \(1\) reducing end, or in NCERT Exemplar terminology, the number of non-reducing ends (or total free ends counting the main chain) is equal to the number of branches plus one.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, the number of 'ends' in a glycogen molecule is equal to the number of branches plus one.

answer.text: Equal to the number of branches plus one
Equal to the number of branch points
Two, one on the left side and another on the right side

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q13 - Number of ends in protein primary structure

questiontext.text: The primary structure of a protein molecule has

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The primary structure of a protein refers to the linear sequence of amino acids linked together by peptide bonds to form a polypeptide chain.

Step 2: Evaluation
In a linear polypeptide chain, the first amino acid (at the left end) retains a free amino group and is called the N-terminal amino acid, while the last amino acid (at the right end) retains a free carboxyl group and is called the C-terminal amino acid. Thus, a single polypeptide chain in its primary structure has two distinct ends.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the primary structure of a protein molecule has two ends.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q14 - Reaction not enzyme-mediated in biological system

questiontext.text: Enzymes are biocatalysts. They catalyse biochemical reactions. In general they reduce activation energy of reactions. Many physico-chemical processes are enzyme mediated. Which of the following reactions is not enzyme-mediated in biological system?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Most biochemical reactions inside living cells are catalysed by specific enzymes that lower the activation energy barrier and accelerate the reaction rate.

Step 2: Evaluation
Untwining the two strands of DNA is catalysed by DNA helicase/topoisomerase; hydrolysis of sucrose into glucose and fructose is catalysed by sucrase (invertase); and formation of peptide bonds during protein synthesis is catalysed by peptidyl transferase (a ribozyme). On the other hand, dissolving CO2 in water is a physical dissolution process that can occur without any enzyme (though the subsequent hydration of CO2 to carbonic acid is accelerated by carbonic anhydrase).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, dissolving CO2 in water is not enzyme-mediated in a biological system.
